title: Ethiopian Infused Honey
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Herb-Infused Honey — Ethiopian mountain honey gently warmed with dried sacred basil (besobela), rue (tena adam), and a cinnamon stick. The aromatic honey used in coffee, on breads, and as a medicine. Ethiopia's herb-infused honey tradition.
longDesc: Herb-infused honey is part of Ethiopia's ancient tradition of medicinal foods — the sacred basil and rue infused into honey produce a condiment with both extraordinary flavour and significant antimicrobial and digestive properties.
ingredients: 2 sprigs dried sacred basil (besobela) — or regular dried basil
steps: Warm honey very gently over lowest heat — it must not boil (above 40°C destroys enzymes).
Keep below 40°C for 8—10 minutes — the honey should feel warm, not hot.
Remove from heat. Allow to cool with herbs still in.
Transfer to a jar. Leave herbs in for 24 hours.
Strain out herbs or leave them in (leaves are edible).
chefTips: Never boil honey — it destroys the enzymes and kills the flavour.
Ethiopian raw honey is already complex — the herbs add another layer, not a replacement.
commonMistakes: Overheating — damages the honey's active compounds.
cookingScience: Raw honey contains glucose oxidase (produces hydrogen peroxide — antimicrobial), invertase (digests sucrose), and numerous volatile aromatic compounds. All are deactivated above 40—45°C. The gentle infusion carries the herb volatile compounds (linalool from basil, rutin from rue) into the honey without destroying its active properties.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian mountain honey from traditional log hives — one of the world's finest honey traditions.
storage: Indefinitely at room temperature — honey does not spoil.
healthBenefits: Raw honey's antimicrobial and antioxidant properties.
One of Ethiopia's most important traditional medicines.
culturalNote: Ethiopian herb-infused honey sits at the intersection of food and medicine — it is given to those with coughs and sore throats, drizzled into coffee as a tonic, spread on celebration breads as a blessing. The besobela (sacred basil) that is infused into it is the same plant used in Ethiopian Orthodox church ceremonies.
